07-01.script:
On the first of July in 1867, three British colonies joined together to form a new country, the Dominion of Canada. Canadians celebrate with fireworks, maple leaves and parties from coast to coast.

In 1858, at the Linnean Society in London, papers by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace were read aloud, explaining evolution by natural selection. Neither man was there, and the audience barely reacted. The president remarked that the year had seen no striking discoveries.

In 1863, the Battle of Gettysburg began in Pennsylvania, three days that would turn the American Civil War.

In 1903, sixty cyclists set off from Paris on the very first Tour de France.

In 1916, on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, Britain lost more men than on any other day in its history.

And in 1979, Sony released a small blue and silver cassette player with headphones, and suddenly people could carry their music wherever they walked. It was called the Walkman.

In India, today honours doctors, on the birthday of the great physician Bidhan Chandra Roy.

07-02.script:
On the second of July in 1776, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia voted to declare the American colonies free and independent. John Adams wrote to his wife that this day would be celebrated with parades and bonfires for ever. He was off by two days: the Declaration would be adopted on the fourth.

In 1900, above Lake Constance in Germany, a long silver cigar of a craft rose slowly into the sky. Count Zeppelin's first airship was flying.

In 1937, the aviator Amelia Earhart and her navigator vanished over the Pacific while trying to fly around the world. No trace of them has ever been confirmed.

In 1962, in Rogers, Arkansas, a shopkeeper named Sam Walton opened the first Walmart store.

And in 1964, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, outlawing discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin. Martin Luther King Jr. stood behind him as he signed.

Today is also World UFO Day, for everyone who has ever looked up at the night sky and wondered.

07-03.script:
On the third of July in 1608, the French explorer Samuel de Champlain built a wooden trading post beside the great St Lawrence River. It would grow into the city of Quebec.

In 1863, on the last day at Gettysburg, General Lee sent twelve thousand men marching across an open field towards the Union lines. Pickett's Charge was cut to pieces, and the tide of the Civil War turned.

In 1886, in Mannheim, Karl Benz drove his three-wheeled motor car down a public road for the first time.

In 1928, John Logie Baird gave the world's first demonstration of colour television in London.

In 1938, the sleek blue steam locomotive Mallard raced down a slope in England at two hundred and three kilometres an hour. No steam engine has ever gone faster.

In 1944, Soviet forces liberated Minsk, and Belarus marks its Independence Day.

And in 1971, the singer Jim Morrison of the Doors was found dead in Paris, aged twenty-seven.

facts.text: Mallard's 1938 run at 126 miles an hour is still the speed record for a steam locomotive.

07-04.script:
On the fourth of July in 1054, Chinese astronomers saw a new star blaze in the constellation of Taurus, so bright it was visible in daylight for weeks. Today, its remains are the glowing Crab Nebula.

In 1776, in Philadelphia, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence: we hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal. Americans celebrate with fireworks, parades and picnics.

Exactly fifty years later, on the fourth of July in 1826, two of its authors, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, died within hours of each other.

In 1845, Henry David Thoreau moved into a small cabin he had built by Walden Pond, to live simply.

In 1862, on a boat trip on the Thames, a mathematician named Charles Dodgson began telling a little girl named Alice a story about falling down a rabbit hole.

In 1939, the baseball star Lou Gehrig, dying of a terrible illness, told a packed Yankee Stadium that he considered himself the luckiest man on the face of the Earth.

And in 2012, physicists at CERN announced they had found the Higgs boson, a particle that helps give everything mass.

07-05.script:
On the fifth of July in 1687, Isaac Newton's Principia was published in London. In it, he showed that the same force that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in its orbit. The universe, it seemed, ran on laws that could be understood.

In 1811, Venezuela declared its independence from Spain, the first Spanish colony in South America to do so.

In 1841, a young preacher named Thomas Cook organised a special train to take five hundred people to a temperance meeting, for a shilling each. It was the beginning of the package tour.

In 1946, at a swimming pool in Paris, a designer named Louis Réard showed a daring two-piece swimsuit. He named it after Bikini Atoll, where atomic bombs had just been tested.

In 1948, Britain's National Health Service was born, promising care free to all who needed it.

In 1962, Algeria declared its independence after eight years of war.

And in 1996, in a laboratory in Scotland, a lamb named Dolly was born, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

07-06.script:
On the sixth of July in 1415, at Constance in Germany, the Czech preacher Jan Hus was burned at the stake for his teachings. A hundred years later, Martin Luther would say: we are all Hussites now.

In 1535, Sir Thomas More, who had refused to accept Henry the Eighth as head of the Church, was beheaded. He told the crowd he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

In 1885, in Paris, Louis Pasteur gave a nine-year-old boy named Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog, the first injections of his new rabies vaccine. The boy lived.

In 1942, in Amsterdam, Anne Frank and her family moved into the secret rooms behind a bookcase, where they would hide for two years.

In 1957, at a church fête in Liverpool, a sixteen-year-old named John Lennon was introduced to a fifteen-year-old named Paul McCartney. Paul showed him how to tune a guitar.

And on that same day, Althea Gibson became the first Black player to win Wimbledon.

07-07.script:
On the seventh of July, people in Japan celebrate Tanabata, the Star Festival. Legend says two lovers, the weaver princess and the cowherd, are separated by the Milky Way and may meet only on this one night of the year. Children write wishes on strips of coloured paper and hang them on bamboo branches.

In 1865, four people convicted of conspiring to kill Abraham Lincoln were hanged in Washington.

In 1928, in the small town of Chillicothe, Missouri, a bakery began selling something new: bread already sliced by a machine. People said it was the greatest thing since, well, nothing.

In 1930, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, died at his home in Sussex.

In 1937, a skirmish at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing began the long war between China and Japan.

In 1981, a solar-powered aircraft called the Solar Challenger flew across the English Channel, powered by sunlight alone.

And in 1985, a seventeen-year-old German named Boris Becker became the youngest man ever to win Wimbledon.

Today is also World Chocolate Day. You may wish to celebrate.

07-08.script:
On the eighth of July in 1497, four small ships sailed out of Lisbon under the command of Vasco da Gama. Their goal was India, by sea, around the bottom of Africa. Ten months later, they would arrive.

In 1709, at Poltava in Ukraine, Peter the Great's Russian army crushed the invading Swedes of King Charles the Twelfth. Russia had become a great power.

In 1776, in the yard of the State House in Philadelphia, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud to the public for the first time, and church bells rang out across the city.

In 1853, four American warships, belching black smoke, steamed into Edo Bay. Commodore Matthew Perry had come to open Japan to the world after two centuries of isolation.

In 1889, the first issue of the Wall Street Journal was published.

In 1947, a newspaper in New Mexico reported that the army had recovered a flying disc near Roswell. The next day, the army said it was a weather balloon. People are still arguing.

And in 2011, the Space Shuttle Atlantis rose into the sky for the last time, ending thirty years of shuttle flights.

07-09.script:
On the ninth of July in 1816, in the city of San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina declared its independence from Spain. Argentines celebrate with flags of sky blue and white.

In 1877, at the All England Croquet and Lawn Tennis Club in Wimbledon, twenty-two gentlemen began the first lawn tennis championship. The winner, Spencer Gore, thought the game would never catch on.

In 1893, in Chicago, a Black surgeon named Daniel Hale Williams opened the chest of a man stabbed in the heart and repaired the wound. It was one of the first successful heart operations.

In 1922, the swimmer Johnny Weissmuller, who would later play Tarzan, became the first person to swim a hundred metres in less than a minute.

In 1955, Bertrand Russell and Albert Einstein, with other great scientists, issued a manifesto warning the world about the danger of nuclear war. Remember your humanity, they wrote, and forget the rest.

And in 2011, South Sudan became the world's newest country.

07-10.script:
On the tenth of July in 1856, in a village in what is now Croatia, Nikola Tesla was born. He would dream up the alternating current that powers our homes, and imagine wireless power and radio long before others.

In 1913, at Furnace Creek in California's Death Valley, a thermometer recorded fifty-six point seven degrees Celsius, the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth.

In 1925, in a small courthouse in Dayton, Tennessee, the trial of a teacher named John Scopes began. He was accused of teaching evolution. The whole world was watching.

In 1938, Howard Hughes took off from New York to fly around the world. He would be back in less than four days.

In 1940, German planes attacked shipping in the English Channel, and the Battle of Britain began.

And in 1962, America launched Telstar, a shining satellite covered in solar cells, which would soon carry live television across the Atlantic for the first time.

07-11.script:
On the eleventh of July in 1302, near the Flemish city of Kortrijk, an army of townsmen and craftsmen on foot defeated the knights of France. They collected hundreds of golden spurs from the fallen, and called it the Battle of the Golden Spurs.

In 1804, on the cliffs at Weehawken, New Jersey, the Vice President of the United States, Aaron Burr, fought a duel with Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton was mortally wounded.

In 1893, in Japan, Kokichi Mikimoto saw the first cultured pearl form inside an oyster he had carefully seeded.

In 1960, Harper Lee published To Kill a Mockingbird, a story of justice and childhood in a small Alabama town, seen through the eyes of a girl called Scout.

In 1979, Skylab, America's first space station, fell back to Earth, scattering pieces across the Australian outback. A town in Western Australia playfully fined NASA for littering.

On this day in 1987, the world's population reached five billion people, and World Population Day was born.

07-12.script:
On the twelfth of July in 1543, at Hampton Court Palace, King Henry the Eighth married his sixth and last wife, Catherine Parr. She would outlive him.

In 1690, on the River Boyne in Ireland, the Protestant King William the Third defeated the Catholic King James the Second. In Northern Ireland, the twelfth of July is still marked with marches.

In 1862, President Lincoln signed a law creating the Medal of Honor, America's highest award for bravery.

In 1962, at the Marquee Club in London, a new band played its first gig. They called themselves the Rolling Stones.

In 1984, Geraldine Ferraro became the first woman chosen to run for Vice President on a major party ticket in the United States.

And in 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope sent back its first full-colour pictures: glittering galaxies, glowing nebulae and the deep, ancient light of the early universe.

Today is also Malala Day, the birthday of Malala Yousafzai, who was shot for wanting girls to go to school, and lived to speak for them all.

07-13.script:
On the thirteenth of July in 1787, the American Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance, setting rules for new states in the west and banning slavery there.

In 1793, in Paris, the revolutionary journalist Jean-Paul Marat was stabbed in his bath by a young woman named Charlotte Corday. The painter Jacques-Louis David turned the scene into a famous painting.

In 1832, the explorer Henry Schoolcraft was guided by an Ojibwe man named Ozawindib to a small lake in Minnesota: the source of the mighty Mississippi.

In 1923, a giant sign was put up on a hill above Los Angeles, advertising houses for sale. It read Hollywoodland. Later the last four letters were removed.

In 1930, in Montevideo, the first FIFA World Cup began, with thirteen teams.

And in 1985, the musicians Bob Geldof and Midge Ure brought together the biggest names in rock for Live Aid, two great concerts in London and Philadelphia, watched by more than a billion people, to raise money for the hungry in Ethiopia.

07-14.script:
On the fourteenth of July in 1789, an angry crowd in Paris stormed the Bastille, a grim old fortress and prison that stood for the king's power. They found just seven prisoners inside. But the fall of the Bastille became the symbol of the French Revolution, and France celebrates its national day with fireworks and a parade down the Champs-Élysées.

In 1865, the English climber Edward Whymper and his party became the first to stand on the summit of the Matterhorn. On the way down, a rope broke, and four of them fell to their deaths.

In 1867, Alfred Nobel demonstrated his new explosive, dynamite, in a quarry in England.

In 1960, a young Englishwoman named Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe in Tanzania to study chimpanzees. She would stay for decades.

And in 2015, after a journey of nine and a half years, NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto and showed us its heart, a vast pale plain shaped like a heart on its surface.

07-15.script:
On the fifteenth of July in 1099, after a long siege, the knights of the First Crusade broke into Jerusalem.

In 1662, King Charles the Second granted a royal charter to a club of curious gentlemen who met to perform experiments and share discoveries. The Royal Society is still one of the great scientific academies of the world.

In 1799, a French soldier digging in the Nile delta near the town of Rosetta found a black stone carved with the same words in three scripts. The Rosetta Stone would be the key that unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs.

In 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte surrendered to the captain of HMS Bellerophon, and was taken into exile for the last time.

In 1916, a timber merchant in Seattle named William Boeing founded a small aircraft company.

And in 1975, a Soviet Soyuz and an American Apollo were launched within hours of each other. Two days later, they met and docked high above the Earth, and the old rivals shook hands in space.

In England, legend says that if it rains on St Swithin's Day, it will rain for forty days more.

07-16.script:
On the sixteenth of July in 1945, before dawn in the New Mexico desert, scientists of the Manhattan Project watched the sky turn whiter than noon. The Trinity test was the first explosion of a nuclear weapon, and the world was never quite the same.

Twenty-four years later to the day, nearly a million people gathered near Cape Kennedy to watch a Saturn Five rocket rise on a pillar of fire. Apollo Eleven was on its way to the Moon.

In 1790, the American Congress chose a stretch of land by the Potomac River for a new capital city, Washington.

In 1935, in Oklahoma City, drivers met a strange new machine on the pavement: the world's first parking meter.

And in 1994, the first fragments of Comet Shoemaker–Levy Nine slammed into Jupiter, leaving dark scars bigger than the Earth. For the first time, astronomers watched two worlds collide.

Today is also World Snake Day.

facts.text: Watching the Trinity fireball, Robert Oppenheimer recalled a line from the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."
Shoemaker–Levy 9 was torn into more than twenty pieces by Jupiter's gravity before it crashed.

07-17.script:
On the seventeenth of July in 1955, Walt Disney opened the gates of a theme park built on orange groves in Anaheim, California. It was chaos: the asphalt was so fresh that women's heels sank into it, the drinking fountains were dry, and thousands arrived with forged tickets. Yet Disneyland soon became the happiest place on Earth.

In 1902, a young engineer named Willis Carrier finished drawings for a machine to control the humidity in a Brooklyn printing works. It was the first modern air conditioner.

In 1918, in the city of Yekaterinburg, the last Russian Tsar and his family were executed in a cellar.

In 1959, Mary Leakey spotted a fossil skull in Olduvai Gorge, and pushed the story of our ancestors far deeper into the past.

And in 1975, an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz docked in orbit, and their crews shook hands through an open hatch.

Today is World Emoji Day, and if you look closely, the calendar emoji says July the seventeenth.

facts.text: World Emoji Day falls on 17 July because that is the date shown on Apple's calendar emoji.
Carrier's first air conditioner was built to stop paper swelling in a printing works, not to cool people.

07-18.script:
On the eighteenth of July in 1918, in a small village in South Africa's Eastern Cape, a boy was born who would spend twenty-seven years in prison and walk out to become his country's first Black president. Nelson Mandela's birthday is now a day of service across the world.

In the year 64, a fire broke out near the Circus Maximus in Rome. It burned for six days and destroyed much of the city. Legend says the emperor Nero played music while it burned.

In 1947, the British parliament's Indian Independence Act received royal assent, setting the date for freedom less than a month later.

In 1968, two engineers in California founded a small company to make memory chips. They called it Intel.

In 1976, at the Montreal Olympics, a fourteen-year-old Romanian gymnast named Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect ten in Olympic history.

And in 1980, India launched its own satellite on its own rocket, joining a small club of spacefaring nations.

events.text: The Great Fire of Rome begins.

facts.text: Mandela Day asks everyone to give 67 minutes of service, one for each year Mandela spent in public life.

07-19.script:
On the nineteenth of July in 1545, King Henry the Eighth stood on the shore at Portsmouth and watched his favourite warship, the Mary Rose, heel over and sink as she sailed out to fight the French. Four hundred and thirty-seven years later, she was raised from the mud of the Solent.

In 1588, lookouts off the coast of Cornwall sighted the sails of the Spanish Armada, and beacon fires carried the news across England.

In 1843, the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel launched the SS Great Britain, the first iron-hulled, propeller-driven ship to cross the Atlantic.

In 1848, in the small town of Seneca Falls, New York, three hundred people gathered for the first women's rights convention, and declared that all men and women are created equal.

In 1900, the first line of the Paris Métro opened.

And in 1969, the Indian government nationalised fourteen of the country's largest banks overnight, changing the face of Indian banking.

births.text: Mangal Pandey, Indian soldier and rebel

facts.text: The raising of the Mary Rose in 1982 was watched live on television by around 60 million people.
The Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments was signed by 68 women and 32 men.
Mangal Pandey's revolt at Barrackpore in 1857 is remembered as an opening spark of India's First War of Independence.

07-20.script:
On the twentieth of July in 1969, a spidery spacecraft called Eagle drifted down towards a plain of grey dust called the Sea of Tranquillity. Alarms were flashing, the fuel was running low, and Neil Armstrong took the controls himself to steer past a field of boulders. Then a calm voice reached Houston: "The Eagle has landed." Mission control, holding its breath, finally exhaled.

Seven years later to the day, the Viking One lander touched down on Mars and sent back the first clear photograph from the surface of the red planet.

In 1810, the people of Bogotá rose against Spanish rule, and Colombia celebrates today as its independence day.

In 1924, chess players from around the world founded FIDE in Paris, which is why today is International Chess Day.

And in 1944, a group of German officers hid a bomb in a briefcase beneath Adolf Hitler's map table. It exploded, but Hitler survived, and the plotters paid with their lives.

facts.text: When Eagle landed, it had less than a minute of descent fuel left before the crew would have had to abort.
The United Nations declared 20 July International Moon Day in 2021.

07-21.script:
On the twenty-first of July in 1969, just before three o'clock in the morning by Greenwich time, Neil Armstrong climbed down the ladder of the lunar module and pressed his boot into the dust of the Moon. "That's one small step for man," he said, "one giant leap for mankind." Six hundred million people were watching on television.

In 1831, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg swore an oath as the first King of the Belgians, and Belgium celebrates its national day.

In 1960, Sirimavo Bandaranaike became Prime Minister of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, the first woman in the world to lead a government.

In 1983, at the Russian research station Vostok in Antarctica, the thermometer fell to minus eighty-nine point two degrees, the coldest temperature ever measured on the ground.

And in 2011, the space shuttle Atlantis glided home to Florida for the last time, bringing thirty years of shuttle flights to an end.

births.text: Paul Julius Reuter, founder of Reuters

facts.text: Armstrong later said he meant to say "one small step for a man".
The footprints left on the Moon could last for millions of years, because there is no wind to blow them away.

07-22.script:
On the twenty-second of July in 1947, in the Constituent Assembly in New Delhi, India adopted its national flag: saffron, white and green, with the blue wheel of Ashoka at its heart. Three weeks later it would fly over a free nation.

In 1933, the American pilot Wiley Post landed in New York after flying alone around the world in seven days and nineteen hours, the first person ever to do so.

In 1944, delegates from forty-four nations finished their talks at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire and created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

In 1962, a single missing symbol in its guidance software sent NASA's Mariner One off course, and it had to be destroyed minutes after launch.

And in 2009, the Moon slid in front of the Sun over India and China, and for more than six minutes the day turned to night. It was the longest total solar eclipse of the twenty-first century.

Today is also Pi Approximation Day, because twenty-two divided by seven is very nearly pi.

births.text: Alex Trebek, Canadian-American game show host

facts.text: 22 divided by 7 is 3.142857…, accurate to pi within about four parts in ten thousand.
The wheel on India's flag has 24 spokes.

07-23.script:
On the twenty-third of July in 1927, a radio station in Bombay went on the air for the Indian Broadcasting Company. From those crackling beginnings grew All India Radio, and India marks today as National Broadcasting Day.

It is also the birthday of two great figures of India's freedom struggle: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, born in 1856, who declared that self-rule was his birthright, and Chandra Shekhar Azad, born in 1906, who vowed never to be taken alive by the British.

In 1903, a dentist in Chicago became the first customer of the new Ford Motor Company, buying a Model A.

In 1914, Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum so harsh it was meant to be refused, and Europe slid towards war.

In 1952, army officers in Egypt overthrew King Farouk.

And in 1962, the satellite Telstar carried the first live television pictures across the Atlantic, and viewers in Europe watched America in real time.

births.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Indian freedom fighter

facts.text: Tilak's famous call was: "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it!"
Azad took the name 'Azad', meaning 'free', and kept his vow never to be captured alive.

07-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of July in 1911, a Peruvian farmer led an American lecturer named Hiram Bingham up a steep, rainy mountainside above the Urubamba River. At the top, wrapped in vines, stood the stone terraces and temples of an Inca city. The world would come to know it as Machu Picchu.

In 1847, Brigham Young looked out over the valley of the Great Salt Lake and is said to have declared, "This is the right place." Utah still celebrates Pioneer Day.

In 1783, Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas. He would free six countries from Spanish rule.

In 1969, the Apollo Eleven capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, and the first moonwalkers came safely home.

And in 1991, in New Delhi, India's finance minister Manmohan Singh presented a budget that opened up the economy. Quoting Victor Hugo, he said no power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come.

births.text: Jennifer Lopez, American singer and actress

facts.text: Machu Picchu was never found by the Spanish conquerors, which is why it survived so well.
Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar.
Machu Picchu sits about 2,430 metres above sea level.

07-25.script:
On the twenty-fifth of July in 1909, at dawn, the French aviator Louis Blériot took off from a field near Calais in a little monoplane with no compass. Thirty-seven minutes later he crash-landed in a meadow beside Dover Castle. He was the first to fly across the English Channel, and Britain was no longer quite an island.

In 1978, in a hospital near Manchester, a baby girl named Louise Brown was born. She was the world's first child conceived by in vitro fertilisation, and since then millions more have followed.

In 1984, the Soviet cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya became the first woman to walk in space.

In 1965, at the Newport Folk Festival, Bob Dylan plugged in an electric guitar, and some of the crowd booed.

And in India, today is the day new Presidents take their oath. In 2007, Pratibha Patil became the first woman to hold the office.

It is also the birthday, in 1920, of Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray photographs revealed the shape of DNA.

events.text: Henry IV of France converts to Catholicism.

facts.text: Every Indian President since 1977 has been sworn in on 25 July.
Blériot had injured his foot and needed crutches when he flew the Channel.

07-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of July in 1999, India announced that its soldiers had driven intruders from the last of the high ridges above Kargil. For weeks, young soldiers had climbed sheer, frozen slopes at night, under fire, to win back peaks like Tiger Hill. Kargil Vijay Diwas honours the more than five hundred who never came home.

In 1847, Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, declared its independence, the first republic in Africa.

In 1953, a young lawyer named Fidel Castro led an attack on the Moncada barracks in Cuba. It failed, but it gave its name to his revolution.

In 1956, President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt announced that he was taking over the Suez Canal, and a crisis followed.

In 1963, the satellite Syncom Two became the first to orbit in step with the turning Earth, opening the way for modern communications.

And in 1971, Apollo Fifteen set off for the Moon, carrying a car folded up in its side.

facts.text: Some of the Kargil battles were fought on peaks more than 5,000 metres high.
Captain Vikram Batra's radio signal after capturing a peak in Kargil was "Yeh dil maange more!"

07-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of July in 1866, the giant steamship Great Eastern sailed into a quiet bay in Newfoundland, paying out the last miles of a cable that ran all the way from Ireland. At last a telegraph line crossed the Atlantic for good, and messages that had taken ten days by ship now took minutes.

In 1921, in a laboratory in Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin, and a disease that had been a death sentence became one people could live with.

In 1694, the Bank of England received its royal charter.

In 1940, a rabbit with a carrot first asked, "What's up, Doc?" Bugs Bunny had arrived.

In 1953, after three years of war, an armistice was signed at Panmunjom, and the guns fell silent across Korea, though no peace treaty has ever followed.

And in 2015, India's beloved former President, the scientist A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, died while doing what he loved most, giving a lecture to students.

Abdul Kalam collapsed while lecturing to students at IIM Shillong.
The first transatlantic cable of 1858 failed after only about three weeks.

07-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of July in 1914, one month after the shots in Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Within a week, alliances had dragged in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. The First World War had begun.

In 1821, in the main square of Lima, General José de San Martín proclaimed the independence of Peru.

In 1858, in Bengal, a British official named William Herschel had a local contractor press his inky hand onto a contract. It was one of the first uses of fingerprints to identify a person.

In 1945, on a foggy Saturday morning, a bomber lost in the mist flew into the seventy-ninth floor of the Empire State Building, and the building still stood.

And in 1976, a huge earthquake struck the Chinese city of Tangshan as people slept, one of the deadliest of the twentieth century.

Today is World Hepatitis Day, on the birthday of Baruch Blumberg, who discovered the hepatitis B virus.

births.text: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, American First Lady

facts.text: Baruch Blumberg won the Nobel Prize in 1976 for discovering the hepatitis B virus, which led to a vaccine.
The elevator operator in the Empire State crash survived a fall of 75 storeys when her lift's cables snapped.

07-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of July in 1958, President Eisenhower signed a law creating a new civilian agency to explore space. The Soviet Sputnik had shocked America the year before, and now the race was truly on. The agency was called NASA, and within eleven years it would put people on the Moon.

In 1836, the Arc de Triomphe was finally completed in Paris, thirty years after Napoleon ordered it built.

In 1948, London opened the first Olympic Games since before the war. They were called the Austerity Games, and athletes brought their own towels.

In 1981, around seven hundred and fifty million people watched on television as Prince Charles married Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul's Cathedral.

And in 2005, astronomers announced the discovery of a distant icy world larger than Pluto, later named Eris. Its discovery led to Pluto losing its place as a planet.

Today is International Tiger Day, and India is home to most of the wild tigers left on Earth.

facts.text: J. R. D. Tata received India's first pilot's licence in 1929 and founded the airline that became Air India.
International Tiger Day was agreed at a tiger summit in Saint Petersburg in 2010.

07-30.script:
On the thirtieth of July in 1930, in a brand new stadium in Montevideo, Uruguay played Argentina in the final of the very first football World Cup. Argentina led at half-time, but Uruguay came back to win four goals to two, and the whole country took the next day off.

Thirty-six years later to the day, England beat West Germany at Wembley to win the World Cup, the only time it has done so.

In 1619, the first elected assembly in the American colonies met in a church in Jamestown, Virginia.

In 1945, the cruiser USS Indianapolis, having just delivered parts of the atomic bomb, was torpedoed in the Pacific. Survivors waited four days in shark-filled waters for rescue.

In 1971, Apollo Fifteen landed beside the Apennine mountains on the Moon.

And in 2003, the last of the original Volkswagen Beetles rolled off the line in Mexico, after more than twenty-one million had been built.

Today is the International Day of Friendship.

facts.text: The first World Cup had only 13 teams, and most European sides refused the long sea voyage to Uruguay.
The 1966 Jules Rimet trophy was stolen before the tournament and found under a hedge by a dog named Pickles.

07-31.script:
On the thirty-first of July in 1940, in Pentonville Prison in London, the Indian revolutionary Udham Singh was hanged. Twenty-one years earlier he had seen the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh, and in March 1940 he shot Michael O'Dwyer, who had governed the Punjab at the time. India remembers him as a martyr.

In 1790, the very first United States patent was granted, to Samuel Hopkins, for a better way of making potash.

In 1964, the American probe Ranger Seven sent back thousands of close-up pictures of the Moon in the last minutes before it crashed into the surface.

In 1971, astronauts Dave Scott and Jim Irwin unfolded the Lunar Roving Vehicle and became the first people to drive on the Moon.

In 1880, the great Hindi and Urdu writer Munshi Premchand was born near Varanasi.

And in 1965, J. K. Rowling was born, who gave her most famous character the very same birthday. Harry Potter turns another year older today.
